messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

At 38, Linh Nguyen had built a life that looked fast, competent, and tightly managed from the outside. She worked as a stock broker in a noisy Manhattan office where phones rang across the floor, traders shouted bids, and market alerts burst from speakers without warning. She lived with her partner in a high-rise downtown and had once taken some pride in how well she could tolerate pressure. What brought her to treatment was not a single new incident but the recognition, after many months, that her world had been shrinking around a past she still could not make feel finished.

The stalking had begun after a brief relationship ended. At first it came as repeated messages, then long voicemails left late at night, then appearances that felt impossible to explain away. He seemed to know where she had been, what train she had taken, when she had gone to dinner. More than once she caught the smell of alcohol before she saw him and felt her body go cold, because that odor had become part of how he arrived into her life: outside her building entrance, too close behind her on the sidewalk, once waiting near her car and speaking in a slurred, insistent voice as if he still had a claim on her. The worst moments were not dramatic in a cinematic sense; that was part of what made them so destabilizing. They were made of repetition, intrusion, and the steady collapse of any expectation that she could predict where she would be safe. By the end she was jumping at every sound in the hallway, bracing whenever a sudden crash came from the street below, already scanning for whether he had found her again.

What she has struggled to explain in the months since is that the memory does not sit in the past in an ordinary way. When she talks about those weeks, Linh often pauses and says it sounds exaggerated even to her, “like something that happened to somebody else,” because the extremity of living under constant watch still feels unreal. Yet when it comes back, it does not return as a distant narrative. She feels as though she is back inside it immediately, with the same surge of terror she had when she realized he could appear anywhere. That quality of reliving has made seemingly ordinary moments in the present feel charged with danger. On the trading floor, a burst of shouting or a slammed door can pull her straight into that older fear before she has even oriented herself. Passing someone on the street with alcohol on his breath can make her chest tighten and her mind race to where she can exit. Seeing a cheerful family in a restaurant window or in the lobby of her building can unsettle her in a way she finds hard to justify, because it throws her against a painful sense of distance from normal life; the contrast makes the stalking feel both bizarre and vividly present, as if everyone else belongs to a safer world she somehow lost access to.

Because the memory arrives with such immediacy, Linh has become increasingly preoccupied with avoiding moments that might set it off. At work she keeps one earbud in even when she is not listening to anything, partly to blunt the shock of sudden loud sounds on the floor. She has started taking side streets home to avoid the bars near her apartment, not wanting to catch the smell of liquor drifting out onto the sidewalk. Her partner has noticed that she becomes quiet and withdrawn when they pass families at brunch spots on weekends, her expression flattening as if she has gone somewhere else. Linh knows these reactions look disproportionate, and that awareness has fed her sense that the whole experience is hard to believe, but for her the triggers do not feel symbolic. They feel like openings through which the stalking breaks back into the present.

Over time, this has changed how she lives. In a profession that depends on rapid judgment under pressure, she has become more brittle on days when the office is especially loud, sometimes needing to step into a stairwell to steady herself after a sudden noise sends her heart racing. At home she is more likely to decline social plans if they involve crowded restaurants or drinking. Her partner has tried to reassure her, but Linh has come to dread the look of concern on his face, as though even that confirms how much the stalking still governs her.

By the time she sought help, she was exhausted by the sense that her life was being organized around avoiding reminders of something that still did not feel fully real and yet could seize her body as if it were happening now. What frightened her most was not only the memories themselves but the possibility that she would never again be able to move through ordinary places—a loud office, a sidewalk outside a bar, a weekend street full of families—without feeling hijacked by terror. What she hoped for, tentatively, was not to erase what happened but to have it become unmistakably past.
